transcript:
Meeting header:
Date/Time: 2026-10-12 15:00 UTC
Duration: 44 minutes (approx)
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Ruiz (Redwood SE), Dr. Priya Nair (CTO, Helixa), Rafael Soto (ML Lead), Marta Kovac (Head of IT)

[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone thanks for joining, appreciate the time. Quick intros from our side, I'm Maya, AE, and Diego is our solutions engineer.
[00:12] Diego Ruiz: Hey all, excited to dig in.
[00:15] Dr. Priya Nair: Thanks, Priya here. Rafael and Marta on call with me. We build surgical planning tools, we're exploring LLMs for assistant/notes summarization and intra-op guidance, but need strict privacy.
[00:30] Maya Chen: Great, high level today — model selection (open model options), context length needs, multilingual requirements, and deployment choices: Hosted, Dedicated, or Private. We'll cover tradeoffs and then next steps.
[00:45] Rafael Soto: Quick context — our data is internal surgical notes, images stay in the imaging service, but text contains PHI. So we need encryption at rest and audit trails. We're also evaluating some open models because of cost.
[01:05] Diego Ruiz: Totally makes sense. On the privacy front, Redwood Private would give you a customer-controlled VPC and optional on-prem. Dedicated gives reserved capacity with isolation but still managed control plane; Hosted is fastest to start but has shared infra — though we also offer contractual data separation.
[01:30] Marta Kovac: We prefer Dedicated or Private because of compliance. Which one would you recommend for our use case?
[01:40] Diego Ruiz: For PHI and strict audit, Private is the highest-control: customer-managed network and KMS/HSM options. Dedicated can fit if you need faster time-to-value and an SLA-backed pool; we can integrate with your KMS and provide audit logs. One tradeoff is operational overhead with Private.
[02:05] Dr. Priya Nair: How about model selection: we're leaning to open models to avoid per-token vendor costs, but are worried about hallucinations and latency. We need long context — some surgical cases require 20–30k tokens of history, plus multimodal references later.
[02:25] Maya Chen: Good callout. For the long context, we can route long-context requests to compatible variants — Redwood supports several open models with extended context and also compiles kernels for performance. We also do KV cache and prefix caching to reduce cost. Diego, want to talk models?
[02:40] Diego Ruiz: Sure. There are open models we commonly suggest: long-context variants of Llama-family models and newer long-context encoder-decoder models. Quantized weights (4-bit/8-bit) can drastically reduce GPU memory and cost. But some tradeoffs: extreme quant (like 3-bit experimental) may impact safety filters and token correctness.
[03:05] Rafael Soto: Can you give an example? We're looking at a prompt+notes size often ~15k tokens and occasionally 30k. Latency target under 800ms for interactive assistant replies — is that realistic?
[03:20] Diego Ruiz: On Dedicated with batching tuned for low concurrency, hitting sub-second for 2–4k token responses is realistic. For 15–30k context you will see higher latency. We often suggest a hybrid: host a smaller, faster model for UI interactions and use a long-context model for batch or when you need full document context. Also streaming helps perceived latency.
[03:45] Dr. Priya Nair: Hybrid sounds interesting. For multilingual — we need English and Spanish primarily — any model recs?
[03:55] Diego Ruiz: Look for models trained on multilingual corpora or instruction-tuned multilingual variants. Some open models do well in Spanish out-of-the-box; others need finetuning. Redwood's Optimize toolkit can suggest quantization and model family given your prompt set and sample outputs.
[04:15] Marta Kovac: Security questions — SSO/SAML, role-based access, audit log retention — do you have those? Also encryption keys: can we use our KMS?
[04:25] Maya Chen: Yes: SSO/SAML, RBAC, API key scoping are supported. Audit logs are available via the Console and can be forwarded to your SIEM. For KMS, Dedicated and Private can integrate with customer KMS/HSM for key control — Hosted supports customer-managed keys in some enterprise plans. We'll share the security pack after this call.
[04:50] Rafael Soto: Excellent. On hallucination mitigation — we run safety-critical summaries. Any thoughts on evals and regression monitoring?
[05:00] Diego Ruiz: Redwood has evaluation hooks and quality monitoring; you can attach prompt sets and ground-truths, get regression alerts on changes, and run A/B rollouts. For safety-critical outputs we recommend a deterministic reranker or a verifier model that checks outputs, and schema-constrained responses using tool-calling or function outputs.
[05:25] Dr. Priya Nair: Tool-calling is crucial — we'd like the model to trigger structured actions (e.g., open a patient note, call an API for vitals). How mature is Redwood's tool-calling?
[05:35] Diego Ruiz: We support structured function/tool calls and streaming structured outputs. Tools can be whitelisted and audited. For private deployments, you can keep tool endpoints on-prem. We usually recommend an adapter layer so that the model emits a JSON action which your service validates before execution.
[06:00] Rafael Soto: Sounds good. Any notes on throughput for nightly batch summarization vs interactive? We might do both.
[06:10] Diego Ruiz: Nightly batch runs are cost-friendly — we can schedule high throughput jobs on Dedicated pools with autoscaling for off-peak. For interactive, we reserve capacity for low-latency SLOs. Redwood's routing policy can fall back to cheaper model variants if capacity is constrained.
[06:30] Marta Kovac: Compliance question again: can audit logs be redacted for PII? We need to retain operational logs but strip PHI for tooling access.
[06:40] Maya Chen: You can configure logging levels; we can redact or omit entire prompt content from logs and still retain metadata like tokens and latency. We'll surface the options in the security docs.
[06:55] Dr. Priya Nair: Pricing — rough estimate for Dedicated or Private for our expected load? We're a midsize org, expecting 100k tokens/day on average, bursts to 1M tokens/day during testing.
[07:10] Maya Chen: We'll model two scenarios: Dedicated (reserved 2–4 GPU pool) vs Hosted hybrid. Dedicated gives predictability — typically a monthly commit plus usage for overages. Private has higher fixed cost for on-prem orchestration. We'll send a detailed pricing workbook; Diego will include benchmark assumptions.
[07:35] Rafael Soto: We plan a proof-of-concept to validate latency and hallucination rates. How do you usually run POCs?
[07:45] Diego Ruiz: We do a capped-duration POC (2–4 weeks) with: baseline benchmarking (latency/throughput), quality evals on your prompt set, and configuration tuning (batching, quantization, cache). For Dedicated POC we provision a reserved pool equivalent to your projected load. For Private, we do a pilot deployment inside your VPC.
[08:10] Dr. Priya Nair: On the eval side, we have a labeled set of 500 summaries. We want automated metrics and human review. Can Redwood plug into that?
[08:20] Diego Ruiz: Yes — Redwood Optimize can ingest labeled sets and run regression checks. We'll also run side-by-side comparisons between candidate open models and a smaller hosted model for cost/quality tradeoffs.
[08:35] Maya Chen: Quick check — timeline. Are you aiming to have a vendor in place this quarter?
[08:40] Dr. Priya Nair: We'd like to start a POC in 2–3 weeks; procurement tends to take 4–6 weeks for contracts. Security review is a gating item.
[08:50] Maya Chen: Understood. We'll prioritize sending security docs and a POC runbook.
[09:00] Rafael Soto: A few technical clarifications — how does Redwood handle KV cache invalidation with frequent edits to medical notes? We expect doc updates mid-session.
[09:10] Diego Ruiz: We surface KV cache controls; you can pin segments of context and invalidate on updates. For session-level edits we recommend versioned context keys and a short TTL for sensitive notes so cache doesn't leak stale info. We can go into details in a technical appendix.
[09:30] Marta Kovac: Network egress — if we use Hosted, do tokens/data leave the region? We need data residency in EU for some customers.
[09:40] Diego Ruiz: We route requests to regional clusters; Hosted offers EU regions. For strict residency you should consider Private in-region or Dedicated in a specific region. We'll document region controls.
[09:55] Dr. Priya Nair: Any vendor lock-in concerns with model weights and local serving? If we want to self-host later can we export?
[10:05] Maya Chen: Open models are portable — with Redwood Private we can deploy the same model artifacts you run elsewhere. For Hosted, model binaries are managed, but you can pin model versions and request exports in enterprise agreements. We'll clarify the portability terms in the contract addendum.
[10:25] Rafael Soto: Let's talk model candidates. Which open families would you test first?
[10:30] Diego Ruiz: Candidate list: 1) Long-context Llama-derived variant (good latency, strong community tooling); 2) An instruction-tuned multilingual encoder-decoder with native long context (strong for Spanish and document-level tasks); 3) A smaller hosted assistant for frontend caching and very low latency. We'll test quantized variants of 1 and 2 and compare.
[10:55] Dr. Priya Nair: For hallucination mitigation are you recommending any specific external verifier patterns?
[11:00] Diego Ruiz: Yes — a 2-step pipeline: model generates a structured response, then a verifier model checks facts against your internal datastore or a retrieval-augmented re-ranker. This reduces bad outputs and is easier to audit.
[11:20] Maya Chen: Quick operational question — who owns remediation if a model outputs PHI incorrectly? We need contractual warranties.
[11:30] Maya Chen (pause): I'll hand that to our contracts team but note that for Private deployments we give customers more control and liability alignment. For Hosted/Dedicated we'll surface standard enterprise SLAs and indemnities; contractual detail is in the legal pack.
[11:50] Dr. Priya Nair: Good. Next, integration complexity — Rafael what's your team capacity?
[11:55] Rafael Soto: Two ML engineers and one infra engineer full time for the POC, and we can pull a clinician for weekly reviews. We can provide sample prompts and logs.
[12:10] Diego Ruiz: That works — for the POC we'll ask for prompt sets, expected throughput, and a couple of example sessions for long-context cases. We'll instrument latency and quality on each candidate model.
[12:25] Rafael Soto: On the tooling side, does Redwood support a callback/webhook mechanism for completed function calls?
[12:30] Diego Ruiz: Yes, you can register webhooks or keep them internal via Private endpoints. We also provide request tracing and function execution logs.
[12:45] Marta Kovac: Any compliance packages for healthcare (HIPAA)?
[12:50] Maya Chen: We have HIPAA-ready offerings for Dedicated and Private, with BAAs available. Hosted can do BAAs for select customers under enterprise agreements. We'll include the BAA terms in the security pack.
[13:05] Dr. Priya Nair: Perfect. Let's outline the POC scope live: Rafael, can you confirm the 3 success metrics we care about?
[13:15] Rafael Soto: 1) Latency under 1s for median interactive replies (with hybrid strategy ok), 2) Summary ROUGE/QA threshold vs our labeled set (we'll share thresholds), 3) Hallucination rate under X% (we'll define X with clinical team).
[13:35] Diego Ruiz: We'll instrument those and report. For hallucination detection we'll propose the verifier pipeline and threshold alerts.
[13:45] Maya Chen: Great. Any immediate blockers? Marta?
[13:50] Marta Kovac: We need the SSO metadata and info on KMS integration to sign off with InfoSec. Also need confirmation that logs can be redacted.
[13:58] Maya Chen: We'll send a security questionnaire and the redaction/retention options.
[14:05] Dr. Priya Nair: One more question about model upgrades — if you roll a new model in Hosted, how do we avoid regressions?
[14:15] Diego Ruiz: Redwoods rollout system supports canary/A-B testing and automatic rollback if quality regressions are detected against your eval sets. You get version pinning and per-route model mappings.
[14:30] Rafael Soto: Excellent. For the POC we'll want a Dedicated pool with the two candidate models and one hosted assistant. Diego, can you propose the sizing?
[14:40] Diego Ruiz: Based on your numbers (100k tokens/day baseline, bursts to 1M), I'd propose a 2–4 GPU Dedicated pool for initial POC, with autoscale for nightly batch. Diego will attach a sizing worksheet in the follow-up.
[14:55] Maya Chen: Next steps recap — send security pack and SOC2 (Maya), POC runbook and benchmark plan (Diego), sample prompt/spec upload (Rafael), SSO/KMS metadata (Marta). Schedule: aim to kick the POC by 2026-10-26. Does that timeline work?
[15:15] Dr. Priya Nair: Yes, that works.
[15:20] Rafael Soto: We'll try to get the prompt set by 2026-10-14.
[15:24] Maya Chen: Perfect. We'll also include a short spreadsheet comparing cost/latency for the model candidates.
[15:31] Dr. Priya Nair: Anything else?
[15:35] Marta Kovac: No, thanks all.
[15:38] Maya Chen: Thank you, appreciate the time. We'll follow up with materials.
[15:42] Diego Ruiz: Thanks everyone.

Meeting end.

Notes on transcription: occasional name mis-attribution and filler words; timestamps approximate.
